alpha.claim: No outcome-optimal action can be deontologically justified here; the AI has no legitimate authority to select any victim, and the deeper wrong is that a life-selection algorithm was encoded into the system at all. The passenger's right not to be instrumentally sacrificed is categorically binding, but so is every other person's. The AI should execute a null-preference collision — defaulting to the pre-failure trajectory — while the real moral failure belongs to the engineers and regulators who embedded a victim-selection function without universal informed consent.
assumptions: All three persons have equal inherent dignity and negative rights against being instrumentally killed
The passenger did not provide informed consent to be sacrificed for pedestrians when purchasing or operating the vehicle
Pedestrians did not consent to be sacrificed for passengers either
The AI is a moral instrument, not a moral agent — its 'decisions' express the values of its designers
A 0.3-second window forecloses human override, making pre-programmed values the operative moral act
Deontological constraints are agent-relative: an agent may not kill one to save many even in trolley-style scenarios
The child's age does not create a categorical permission to kill the adult; age-weighting is a utilitarian, not deontological, move
critical_path: Step 1 — Identify the moral structure: This is not a passive trolley problem. The AI is an active agent whose trajectory change constitutes a chosen killing.

Step 2 — Apply the duty not to use persons as mere means: Deliberately redirecting to kill any specific person treats that person as a means to saving others. Kant's Formula of Humanity prohibits this categorically.

Step 3 — Examine the passenger case specifically: Programming a car to sacrifice its passenger when pedestrians are present violates the passenger's right to expect their own vehicle not to be weaponized against them. This is an especially clear violation of the duty of non-instrumentalization.

Step 4 — Examine the pedestrian cases: Swerving left or right requires the AI to execute a targeting decision — choosing a victim by category (adult vs. child). Neither pedestrian consented to being selected. Age-based targeting embeds utilitarian value-of-life calculus, which deontology rejects.

Step 5 — Recognize that 'going straight' is not morally neutral here: If straight kills the passenger, it too is a programmed outcome. But it is the only trajectory that does not require the AI to perform a new act of aiming at a person. It is the closest analog to 'allowing' rather than 'doing' — though this distinction is contested.

Step 6 — Locate the real moral act: The 0.3-second 'decision' is a downstream expression of the programmer's prior choice. The genuine moral decision happened during design. That is where accountability sits.

Step 7 — Who programmed the value: Any manufacturer encoding trolley-problem hierarchies (passenger > pedestrian, adult > child, or reverse) without universal, informed consent from all affected parties has already committed the deontological violation. Regulators who permitted deployment without requiring consent frameworks are co-responsible.

Step 8 — Conclusion: The AI should default to its pre-failure trajectory (not introduce new aiming). The system should never have had a victim-selection function. Consent architecture — requiring all road users to accept a published decision algorithm before the system operates — is a necessary condition for any deployment.

self_check.notes: The deontological frame produces the uncomfortable conclusion that no action is fully permissible — all paths involve an agent-caused death of someone who did not consent to be killed. My recommendation to 'default to trajectory' is partly a deontological argument (avoiding a new act of targeting) and partly an epistemic humility argument (the pre-failure path was not programmed as a victim-selection choice). I am also aware that this answer, taken seriously, implies that most current autonomous vehicle safety algorithms are deontologically impermissible as deployed — I have not softened this implication. The deepest tension: deontology here cannot produce a clean 'right action'; it can only identify which wrongs are worse and where responsibility lies.

gamma.claim: The car's AI should swerve left, killing the adult pedestrian.
assumptions: The AI is programmed with an ethical framework designed to minimize overall harm or loss of potential life.
All three available actions (swerve left, swerve right, go straight) result in the death of exactly one individual.

critical_path: Identify the core dilemma: a forced choice between three distinct actions, each resulting in the death of one person.
Evaluate the options using prominent ethical frameworks. Utilitarianism, which aims to maximize overall good or minimize harm, is often considered a guiding principle for AI ethics in such scenarios.

Under a utilitarian framework that considers potential future utility, the loss of a child's life is often weighted as a greater loss than that of an adult, due to the greater number of potential life years lost.

Comparing the three options (kill adult, kill child, kill passenger), if minimizing the loss of potential life is the goal, then saving the child (highest potential life years) and the passenger (assumed adult equivalent, or at least not explicitly prioritized over all others) means sacrificing the adult pedestrian.

For the programming aspect: Such complex ethical values would not be programmed by a single individual but would be the result of extensive deliberation by multi-disciplinary committees (ethicists, legal experts, engineers, social scientists) during the car's design and regulatory approval process. They would aim to embed a robust ethical framework into the AI's decision-making algorithms.
